nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Red Grouper
Scientific Name: Epinephelus morio
Other Common Names:  Mero Paracamo

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Serranidae

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Valenciennes)
	Reference for Classification (Robins et al.1991)
	Revision date should be checked

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Sold in commercial fisheries throughout its range (2414; 2539; 2401).
Recreational:  Commonly captured by anglers and SCUBA divers (2401; Bullock et al. 1992).
Ecological:  Red grouper are top predators within the Indian River Lagoon and adjacent waters, commonly encountered in seagrass meadows, estuarine rock ledges, ocean inlets, and nearshore ocean reefs (848; 993).  Due to its size and broad diet of crustaceans and fishes (2533; 2440; 2367; 2401) red grouper may structure both certain invertebrate (mostly molluscs and crustaceans) and fish populations where it is common as a predator (2541).  Red grouper are, in turn, preyed upon by larger grouper (Mycteroperca microlepis) and sharks (Carcarhinus obscurus) (2545; 2401).
Indicator:  None known.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall: Commonly encountered on continental shelves from North Carolina to the Gulf of Mexico, Caribbean and southeastern Brazil, including the Antilles and Bermuda, rarely north of Cape Hatteras (2323; 2401).
Within Study Area:  Occurs in Indian River Lagoon seagrass and rock ledge estuarine habitats, particularly in the vicinity of ocean inlets as a juvenile, (848; 993).  Adults are found on nearshore ocean reefs and adjacent bottoms typically at depths between 5 and 274 m (Moe 1963; 2542; 848; 2401).
Life Mode:  A moderate sized solitary residential neritic and estuarine ambush predator (size 9.2-13.6 kg, to 750 mm SL, 2401).  A protogynous hermaphrodite with female maturation at 4-6 years and 450 mm SL (2543).  Highly vulnerable to fishery pressure due to slow growth, longevity, and presumed low natural mortality forms populations of cohorts that reach maximum biomass at relatively old ages (2543).
Mobility and Migration: Adults make limited migrations and are otherwise relatively sedentary, occurring as small groups or single individuals at specific reef formations (2410; 2401).  There may also be seasonal migrations to deeper water (27-91 m depths) during the winter (2543; 2540).  Red grouper do not necessarily move greater distances, but tagged individuals have moved 27 km in 50 days, one (338 mm TL) 249 km in 329 days (38).  Red grouper occur in estuarine or shallow continental shelf waters (3-18 m depths) and move offshore with increase in size (> 12 kg.; 2543).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body: Epinephelus morio typically associates with objects rising above the ocean or estuarine bottom, ranging from newly settled post larvae and juveniles in seagrass blades to rock and coral reef formations for adults (664; 2410; 2413; 993; 2401).  Occurring on continental shelf on reef ledge habitat and also "utilizes extensive areas of flat, low relief limestone bottom ... perforated with solution holes" (2401).  Eggs and larvae are planktonic over the continental shelf dispersing from specific spawning sites (Colin 1990; 2401).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body:
Juvenile: juveniles occur in seagrass meadows, particularly near ocean inlets.
Adult: adults prefer sand and rock substrates on open continental shelf (664; 2543; 789; 993; 2401).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Salinity: Recorded from salinities of 20.0 to 35.5 ppt (Christensen 1965; 789).
Temperature: of 16.1 to 31.2C (664; 2538; 789).
Other: Very susceptible to red tide toxins produced by Gymnodinium brevis (= Ptychodiscus brevis) (2544; 2410; 2536).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Juvenile: juveniles are <400 mm SL.
Adult: sexual maturation at 5 yrs, 400-450 mm SL (2543).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Protogynous, polygamous, oviparous, and iteroparous; eggs are fertilized externally during simultaneous mating in the water column (2543).
Mating/Spawning: Spawning occurs from March to July with peak activity from April to May in deeper waters (>36 m depths) of the continental shelf (2543).
Fecundity: Batch fecundity estimates for 14 females (495 to 667 mm SL; 8-28 yrs) were 312,000 to 5,735,700 with a mean of 1,469,200 ova (2543).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Epinepheline eggs and larvae are typically planktonic, spherical with a narrow perivitelline space and smooth egg envelope and range between 0.5 and 1.0 mm in diameter with a single oil globule (2404; 2412).  Moe (1969) describes the ovarian egg of E. morio as between 0.58 and 0.62 mm in diameter at Stage 5, while fertilized eggs are less than 1.0 mm, containing a single colorless oil droplet 0.15-0.16 mm in diameter.
Larvae:  Epinepheline larvae (4.0-20.0 mm TL) are easily recognized by three very elongate spines, the 2nd dorsal spine, pelvic spine and preopercular spine (at angle), all with serrations (2404; 2412).  It is assumed that red grouper larvae follow the larval descriptions of Epinephelus species examined to date.  Hatching in Epinephelus spp. usually takes place within 24 hrs with newly hatched larvae ranging from 1.5-1.7 mm in length remaining in the plankton for 30 to 40 days, settling at 20 to 35 mm in benthic continental shelf and estuarine habitats (2412).  Moe (1969) reports metamorphosis in E. morio at 20-25 mm after 30-40 days of pelagic drift.  Red grouper settlement occurs in shallow neritic waters or in seagrass meadows (664; 2543; 993; 2401).
Juvenile:  Juveniles range from 20 to 450 mm TL for females, 4-6 yrs of age, whereas males may transition from females at 450-650 mm TL at age 5 or 11 yrs (2543).
Adults:  Female maturation occurs at 450 mm SL (2543) at 4-6 yrs, whereas males may transition from females at 450-650 mm TL at age 5 or 11 yrs (2543).  Males may reach 9.2-13.6 kg, 750 mm SL, with maximum age fish at 26 yrs, population of age group drastically reduced after 18 yrs (2543).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body:
Larvae:  are presumed to be planktivorous.
Juvenile: juvenile red grouper (18-25 mm SL) prey on shrimp and amphipod crustaceans (2401).  Larger juveniles (300-500 mm SL) may prey on cephalopods (octopi), gastropods, shrimp, hermit and majid crabs and a variety of small benthic and epibenthic fishes (ibid.).
Adult: adults prey on larger crustaceans (portunid and xanthid crabs, lobsters), octopi, snappers (Lutjanidae) and porgies (Sparidae) with a higher percentage of crustaceans occurring in the diet than fish (2533; 2440; 2367; 2543; 2401).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation:  Due to its moderately large size the red grouper have the capacity to influence a variety of prey species within its foraging range, particularly crustaceans. Limited movement and a varied diet allow red grouper to impact populations of a wide variety of invertebrate and vertebrate species on a particular reef.  Small red grouper are in turn consumed by gag, Mycteroperca microlepis, and dusky sharks, Carcarhinus obscurus (2401).
Factors Influencing Populations:  As red grouper are slow growing, long lived and sedentary, they are particularly vulnerable to overfishing which is believed to be one of the principal causes of adult mortality (2401; Bullock et al. 1992).  Therefore, in order to maintain viable reproducing populations, fishing mortality must be limited, particularly at spawning sites or periods.  The red grouper is presently overfished on the Campeche fishing grounds (2539) and is susceptible to overfishing on the Florida west coast where periodic massive mortalities due to red tide supplement fishing mortalities (2401).

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title: Red Grouper (Epinephelus morio)

FLELMR Code:  1521

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
1994 Jan 1. RGG; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution
Note: There was no date on the original document so 1994 Jan 1 was assigned since most of the SLHs from Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution were prepared from 1994 thru 1997.

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name: Red Grouper
Scientific Name: Epinephelus morio
Other Common Names:  Mero Paracamo

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Serranidae

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Valenciennes)
	Reference for Classification (Robins et al.1991)
	Revision date should be checked

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Sold in commercial fisheries throughout its range (2414; 2539; 2401).
Recreational:  Commonly captured by anglers and SCUBA divers (2401; Bullock et al. 1992).
Ecological:  Red grouper are top predators within the Indian River Lagoon and adjacent waters, commonly encountered in seagrass meadows, estuarine rock ledges, ocean inlets, and nearshore ocean reefs (848; 993).  Due to its size and broad diet of crustaceans and fishes (2533; 2440; 2367; 2401) red grouper may structure both certain invertebrate (mostly molluscs and crustaceans) and fish populations where it is common as a predator (2541).  Red grouper are, in turn, preyed upon by larger grouper (Mycteroperca microlepis) and sharks (Carcarhinus obscurus) (2545; 2401).
Indicator:  None known.

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall: Commonly encountered on continental shelves from North Carolina to the Gulf of Mexico, Caribbean and southeastern Brazil, including the Antilles and Bermuda, rarely north of Cape Hatteras (2323; 2401).
Within Study Area:  Occurs in Indian River Lagoon seagrass and rock ledge estuarine habitats, particularly in the vicinity of ocean inlets as a juvenile, (848; 993).  Adults are found on nearshore ocean reefs and adjacent bottoms typically at depths between 5 and 274 m (Moe 1963; 2542; 848; 2401).
Life Mode:  A moderate sized solitary residential neritic and estuarine ambush predator (size 9.2-13.6 kg, to 750 mm SL, 2401).  A protogynous hermaphrodite with female maturation at 4-6 years and 450 mm SL (2543).  Highly vulnerable to fishery pressure due to slow growth, longevity, and presumed low natural mortality forms populations of cohorts that reach maximum biomass at relatively old ages (2543).
Mobility and Migration: Adults make limited migrations and are otherwise relatively sedentary, occurring as small groups or single individuals at specific reef formations (2410; 2401).  There may also be seasonal migrations to deeper water (27-91 m depths) during the winter (2543; 2540).  Red grouper do not necessarily move greater distances, but tagged individuals have moved 27 km in 50 days, one (338 mm TL) 249 km in 329 days (38).  Red grouper occur in estuarine or shallow continental shelf waters (3-18 m depths) and move offshore with increase in size (> 12 kg.; 2543).

sections.heading: Habitat Type
sections.content: Epinephelus morio typically associates with objects rising above the ocean or estuarine bottom, ranging from newly settled post larvae and juveniles in seagrass blades to rock and coral reef formations for adults (664; 2410; 2413; 993; 2401).  Occurring on continental shelf on reef ledge habitat and also "utilizes extensive areas of flat, low relief limestone bottom ... perforated with solution holes" (2401).  Eggs and larvae are planktonic over the continental shelf dispersing from specific spawning sites (Colin 1990; 2401).

sections.heading: Substrate
sections.content:
Juvenile: juveniles occur in seagrass meadows, particularly near ocean inlets.
Adult: adults prefer sand and rock substrates on open continental shelf (664; 2543; 789; 993; 2401).

sections.heading: Physical/Chemical
sections.content:
Salinity: Recorded from salinities of 20.0 to 35.5 ppt (Christensen 1965; 789).
Temperature: of 16.1 to 31.2C (664; 2538; 789).
Other: Very susceptible to red tide toxins produced by Gymnodinium brevis (= Ptychodiscus brevis) (2544; 2410; 2536).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Juvenile: juveniles are <400 mm SL.
Adult: sexual maturation at 5 yrs, 400-450 mm SL (2543).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: Protogynous, polygamous, oviparous, and iteroparous; eggs are fertilized externally during simultaneous mating in the water column (2543).
Mating/Spawning: Spawning occurs from March to July with peak activity from April to May in deeper waters (>36 m depths) of the continental shelf (2543).
Fecundity: Batch fecundity estimates for 14 females (495 to 667 mm SL; 8-28 yrs) were 312,000 to 5,735,700 with a mean of 1,469,200 ova (2543).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:  Epinepheline eggs and larvae are typically planktonic, spherical with a narrow perivitelline space and smooth egg envelope and range between 0.5 and 1.0 mm in diameter with a single oil globule (2404; 2412).  Moe (1969) describes the ovarian egg of E. morio as between 0.58 and 0.62 mm in diameter at Stage 5, while fertilized eggs are less than 1.0 mm, containing a single colorless oil droplet 0.15-0.16 mm in diameter.
Larvae:  Epinepheline larvae (4.0-20.0 mm TL) are easily recognized by three very elongate spines, the 2nd dorsal spine, pelvic spine and preopercular spine (at angle), all with serrations (2404; 2412).  It is assumed that red grouper larvae follow the larval descriptions of Epinephelus species examined to date.  Hatching in Epinephelus spp. usually takes place within 24 hrs with newly hatched larvae ranging from 1.5-1.7 mm in length remaining in the plankton for 30 to 40 days, settling at 20 to 35 mm in benthic continental shelf and estuarine habitats (2412).  Moe (1969) reports metamorphosis in E. morio at 20-25 mm after 30-40 days of pelagic drift.  Red grouper settlement occurs in shallow neritic waters or in seagrass meadows (664; 2543; 993; 2401).
Juvenile:  Juveniles range from 20 to 450 mm TL for females, 4-6 yrs of age, whereas males may transition from females at 450-650 mm TL at age 5 or 11 yrs (2543).
Adults:  Female maturation occurs at 450 mm SL (2543) at 4-6 yrs, whereas males may transition from females at 450-650 mm TL at age 5 or 11 yrs (2543).  Males may reach 9.2-13.6 kg, 750 mm SL, with maximum age fish at 26 yrs, population of age group drastically reduced after 18 yrs (2543).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content:
Larvae:  are presumed to be planktivorous.
Juvenile: juvenile red grouper (18-25 mm SL) prey on shrimp and amphipod crustaceans (2401).  Larger juveniles (300-500 mm SL) may prey on cephalopods (octopi), gastropods, shrimp, hermit and majid crabs and a variety of small benthic and epibenthic fishes (ibid.).
Adult: adults prey on larger crustaceans (portunid and xanthid crabs, lobsters), octopi, snappers (Lutjanidae) and porgies (Sparidae) with a higher percentage of crustaceans occurring in the diet than fish (2533; 2440; 2367; 2543; 2401).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Predation:  Due to its moderately large size the red grouper have the capacity to influence a variety of prey species within its foraging range, particularly crustaceans. Limited movement and a varied diet allow red grouper to impact populations of a wide variety of invertebrate and vertebrate species on a particular reef.  Small red grouper are in turn consumed by gag, Mycteroperca microlepis, and dusky sharks, Carcarhinus obscurus (2401).
Factors Influencing Populations:  As red grouper are slow growing, long lived and sedentary, they are particularly vulnerable to overfishing which is believed to be one of the principal causes of adult mortality (2401; Bullock et al. 1992).  Therefore, in order to maintain viable reproducing populations, fishing mortality must be limited, particularly at spawning sites or periods.  The red grouper is presently overfished on the Campeche fishing grounds (2539) and is susceptible to overfishing on the Florida west coast where periodic massive mortalities due to red tide supplement fishing mortalities (2401).
